saetze.text: Introductory Words of Preface
A book that for 2,500 years has held a place among a great nation as a model work upon the art of war must indeed be a work of a most singular nature.
It almost sounds like a fairy tale!
Yet "The Book of War," whose authors are the famous Chinese generals Sun Tzu and Wu Tzu, may justly lay claim to this high honour.
The work dates from the 5th century B.C.
It is still today the most celebrated book that Chinese literature can show upon war and warfare.

Although during the last decades many of our best works treating military matters have been translated into Chinese, these two old masters have nevertheless succeeded in maintaining their ground as classics.

This singular fact is explained first of all by the circumstance that their writings treat chiefly of the fundamental principles of war and warfare, and further of the influence which politics and human nature in general may exercise upon military operations.
It is therefore of great interest to find how unchanging, in the main, the principles and operations of warfare are.
At the time when this work was written, China was a conglomeration of principalities living in constant feud with one another.
Personal ambition and intrigues, not the wishes of the people, were the chief factors in these wars.
One could not rely upon patriotism or any other popular movement to maintain morale among the troops.
General Sun Tzu now expresses in his works the opinion that the morale, or the spirit, of the troops is a wholly decisive factor in war.
One must, he maintains, never make the enemy desperate—he should therefore never be entirely surrounded.
An escape route for flight weakens the resolution of the enemy general and the self-confidence of his troops in a most striking manner.
Truly characteristic of a Chinese army was, as is well known, the great number of standard-bearers.
Their chief purpose was to consist in maintaining the spirit among the troops.
A forest of mighty flags, gaily fluttering in the wind, gave the troops a certain feeling of security—it cheered them, much like a military band.
It must surely be attributed to the fact that the profession of the warrior was never highly esteemed in China, that the sovereign prince only seldom went to war himself.

For the most part he employed a professional who then commanded the army—often one of those "masters of the art of war" who wandered from one state to another and professed to be able to entrust the secret of victory to him who would offer them the greatest sum as reward for their services.
Since, however, war means havoc and devastation, it was of quite essential importance that military operations should be carried out in the enemy's country.
But once one has penetrated thither, a strict offensive is by no means held to be requisite.
In connection with this, Sun Tzu gives the following counsel: "At first behave with the modesty of a young maiden."
Then one should move the enemy to seize the initiative.
If marches have wearied him or he makes a false move, Sun Tzu says: "Then throw yourself upon him with the liveliness of a rabbit."
Both Sun Tzu and Wu Tzu are of the opinion that a defensive-offensive posture is the most advisable.
The general should not engage in the actual battle until the enemy is no longer able to offer successful resistance.
One should, however, beware of a passive defensive.
As regards tactics on the battlefield itself, a regular pitched battle—in other words, a frontal attack—is a proceeding that does no great honour to an able general.
Generally speaking, the plan of attack should be to divide the army into two parts.
While the enemy is thus drawn into battle by the one division, the other strikes him.
The reserve troops, accordingly, are to decide the battle.
This instruction is a striking example of the fact that military principles have in general not changed during the last two thousand years.
Although Sun Tzu as well as Wu Tzu were professional soldiers, both point out that even a successful war is a national misfortune.
Wu Tzu remarks on this: “There are but few who have attained to power on earth through many victories.
Nor should one ever enter upon a war until a careful comparison of the troops arrayed on both sides shows one that victory is wholly certain.”
Great importance is attached to espionage.
Highly honoured by his countrymen stood the spy.
The fact that many of China's national heroes have been spies proves that the part they played was not forgotten.
Often they laboured heavily for years to raise themselves to high rank in the service of the sovereign prince.
The proper handling of a spy belonged to the most difficult tasks of a general.
In earlier times—until the opening of Japan to foreign trade, that is, in 1860/61—Sun Tzu and Wu Tzu stood there in as great, if not even greater, esteem than in China.
For in that land war is regarded as an irksome and unprofitable phase in the national life—victory in a war is not accounted there the greatest heroic deed of a state.
Quite otherwise in Japan.
Many, many generations of its soldiers have been sent into battle according to the counsels of Sun Tzu and Wu Tzu.
A small “army” of commentators has opened up the work from every side.
Naturally it has since had to make way for the scientific works of European writers.
For all that, the counsels which these two authors give in their book may well not have been wholly without influence even in the last two wars which Japan has waged.
The Japanese, at any rate, furnished proof of their words: “It is the energy born of desperation that ever carries off the victory.”
Concerning the lives of the two generals, but little is known.
Patriots, properly speaking, one cannot call them: they were the pure professional strategists, who almost constantly changed their services—now they were employed in this state, now in that.
While Sun Tzu is depicted as a quite estimable character, it is said of Wu Tzu that he was a morally base man.
Yet in the literature of China the pair of authors Sun Tzu and Wu Tzu stand even today as admirable strategists.
Sun Tzu: I. Introductory Thoughts
For all nations, war is a matter of the very highest importance.
Upon the army depend life and death; the standing or the downfall of a state are subject to it.
One should therefore study this matter with the greatest care.
Besides stratagem and a correct understanding of the situation, there is known in war also the so-called "the Way."
By this are understood the virtues: humaneness, propriety, righteousness, wisdom, sense of duty, sincerity, nobility of mind, self-control.
If the sovereign prince is a man who practises the Way, the people likewise will hold together and will not fear dangers.
Thus the services of his subjects are ever at the ruler's disposal.
Yet for all his benevolence, he must not neglect to act strictly according to the laws.
It is of the highest importance that a sovereign prince should constantly compare the condition of neighbouring states hostilely disposed toward him with his own.
But the general, too, must be constantly active; he must seek to turn natural advantages to account, and that even in times of peace.
To these belong discipline in the army, the instruction and training of the troops; and further, justice must prevail, both as regards rewards and punishments.
War is an act of pretext and false grounds, a mask and a stratagem.
If, then, we are in a position to intervene actively, we should feign incapacity.
When near the enemy, we pretend to be far away, while at a great distance we pretend to be near.
Seek ever to put the enemy on a false trail, even if you should thereby forfeit some small advantage.
Throw the adversary into confusion, and then fall upon him.
Pretend to possess great forces, confound him in his plans, and so discompose him.
Feign to be the weaker, and lead him secretly to despise you.
If the enemy is very strong, then weary him.
If great unity prevails in his camp, then seek to bring about a division there.
Attack weak points and appear in unexpected places.
Sun Tzu: II. Military Operations
A campaign requires a good many things.

When the army operates at a great distance from the borders of its country, provisioning often causes great difficulties; the war materiel must also be replenished – and with this, therefore, great expense is bound up.
If the war lasts long, the country often runs short of money to carry it on further.

When the soldiers are then exhausted by their many exertions, and their martial ardour has slackened, when the weapons are worn out and the funds for waging war can no longer be procured, then the neighbouring states often perceive this desperate situation – and fall upon the unhappy country.
Even the most skilful general has never yet gained anything by drawing out operations at length.
In truth, there has never been a country that derived any advantage from a long war.
One must know the ills and disadvantages that attend a war, in order to understand that no profit can be drawn from the same.
A long war also impoverishes the citizens.
The wise general therefore seeks to approach the enemy as soon as may be.
The soldiers must be spurred on to smite the enemy.
Whosoever can gain an advantage over him should be richly rewarded.
The prisoners of war must also be well treated.
The purpose of war is to emerge victorious.
Only no protracted operation, even should one conduct it quite skillfully.
A good general is lord and master over the life of a nation; he is the guardian of the well-being of the whole land.
Sun Tzu: III. Attack by Means of Stratagem
According to the laws of war, one should ever seek to conquer a country, as it were, wholly unobserved.
To overcome it with sword and fire is by no means always advisable.
Far better it is to take the enemy army captive without a stroke of the sword than to defeat it after stubborn resistance.
The highest art of war, then, consists in rendering the enemy harmless without battle.
Note: The Chinese army corps at that time numbered 12,500 men.
It was divided into units of 500 men ("lü"); from these, in turn, squads of 30 men each ("tsu") were formed.
The most skilful army commander, therefore, outwits the enemy by exemplary stratagem.
First, he earns merit who prevents the adversary from uniting his armed forces.
Next comes he who carries out the attack upon the enemy army.
To besiege a fortress is surely the worst resort.
Never undertake a siege if thou canst steer clear of it.
The preparations alone already consume much time.
The further consequence is that the general loses his composure, his patience is exhausted, and many of his soldiers lose their lives to the enemy during the preparations.
Such and similar ills attend sieges.
The art of the army commander, then, consists in rendering the enemy army unfit for battle without any stroke of the sword.
Fortresses, for example, he takes without besieging them; without long struggles he makes himself master of the land.
Herein consists the attack by means of stratagem.

To the rules of war belong the following: If thou art five times as strong as the enemy, then surround him; if thou art three times as strong, then attack him; if the forces are of equal strength, then stake all and fight.
If thou art weaker, then manoeuvre and await the opportunity.
But if thou art wholly and decidedly the weaker, then give the enemy no opportunity to engage thee in battle.
The warrior is the strong pillar of the land.
If he be of iron, then the land also is of necessity strong.
But if the armed forces be insufficient, then the land also is weak.
In many cases one may foretell with fair certainty on which side victory shall be recorded.
To emerge victorious, the general must first know when it is time to fight.
He must also know when small or large bodies of troops are to be sent into the field.
A great artifice, however, consists in going into battle when the enemy is wholly careless and in no wise expects an attack.
Sun Tzu: IV. The Battle Formation
To attack the enemy before one knows with certainty that one can defeat him is not advisable.
But if the soldiers are capable, then one need surely not fear being defeated—the enemy stands there without hope.
Now it may indeed occur that all the preconditions necessary for a victory are present, yet one cannot make use of them.
If a victory appears impossible, then take up the defensive; but if victory is certain, then employ the offensive.
A victory, even if the populace may regard it as such, need not by any means be a true success.
As we already know, the truly capable warrior wins the battle without desperate assaults, naturally under the direction of a wise general.
If he fights at all, this already means "victory"; for he attacks only when the enemy has sown the seed of his own defeat.
First, then, assure oneself of victory, and only then attack.
The army destined for defeat likewise fights, but in the confidence that some unforeseen favourable opportunity may possibly bring victory to its arms.
The victorious host is then like a beam laid upon the scale against a feather.
Its attack might be compared to waters long held back, which suddenly burst through and pour into the valleys.

saetze.kapitel: Suntzu: V. Der Geist der Truppen
saetze.text: Sun Tzu: V. The Spirit of the Troops

saetze.kapitel: Suntzu: V. Der Geist der Truppen
saetze.text: The direction of great masses of troops presents not much greater difficulties than that of smaller ones, provided one divides the former into smaller detachments.

saetze.kapitel: Suntzu: V. Der Geist der Truppen
saetze.text: By means of drum, bell, and flag it is possible to direct even considerable bodies of troops.

saetze.kapitel: Suntzu: V. Der Geist der Truppen
saetze.text: – By skilfully alternating regular and irregular manoeuvres, the army is protected from defeat.

saetze.kapitel: Suntzu: V. Der Geist der Truppen
saetze.text: If one knows the strong and the weak sides of the enemy, and furthermore employs cunning and stratagems, then the foe shall be crushed like an egg upon which one lets fall a millstone.

saetze.kapitel: Suntzu: V. Der Geist der Truppen
saetze.text: Note: The drum was the signal for assembling and advancing, the bell that for halting.

saetze.kapitel: Suntzu: V. Der Geist der Truppen
Suntzu: V. Der Geist der Truppen
saetze.text: When it comes to battle, one attacks the opponent with the “normal” fighting force, but defeats him with the “abnormal.”

saetze.kapitel: Suntzu: V. Der Geist der Truppen
saetze.text: If one handles the abnormal troops in a skilful manner, they are capable of endless variation.

saetze.kapitel: Suntzu: V. Der Geist der Truppen
saetze.text: Their variation resembles the wheel, which has neither beginning nor end.

saetze.kapitel: Suntzu: V. Der Geist der Truppen
saetze.text: The spirit of the troops then resembles the raging plunge of a mountain torrent, which sweeps boulders along with it.

saetze.kapitel: Suntzu: V. Der Geist der Truppen
saetze.text: The combatants strike terror.

saetze.kapitel: Suntzu: V. Der Geist der Truppen
Suntzu: V. Der Geist der Truppen
saetze.text: Yet in the tumult and confusion of battle no disorder is known.

saetze.kapitel: Suntzu: V. Der Geist der Truppen
saetze.text: Yea, even when the fight rages most wildly, the battle formation remains impenetrable.

saetze.kapitel: Suntzu: V. Der Geist der Truppen
Suntzu: V. Der Geist der Truppen
saetze.text: If discipline in the army is perfect, then one may feign want and disorder.

saetze.kapitel: Suntzu: V. Der Geist der Truppen
saetze.text: But if the troops are reckless and fearless, if thou art truly strong, then dissemble as though thou wert weak.

saetze.kapitel: Suntzu: V. Der Geist der Truppen
saetze.text: But we compel the enemy to keep himself in motion by taking up various positions to which he must then conform.

saetze.kapitel: Suntzu: V. Der Geist der Truppen
saetze.text: If we offer the opponent an advantageous point, then he will assuredly make use of it.

saetze.kapitel: Suntzu: V. Der Geist der Truppen
saetze.text: But once thou hast set him in motion, then fall upon him and strike him.

saetze.kapitel: Suntzu: V. Der Geist der Truppen
saetze.text: A capable army commander, in an attack, trusts greatly in the spirit that governs the troops – he does not rely solely upon their proficiency.

saetze.kapitel: Suntzu: V. Der Geist der Truppen
saetze.text: If he sees that an advantage is offered him anywhere, then he exploits it to the uttermost.

saetze.kapitel: Suntzu: V. Der Geist der Truppen
saetze.text: If the general is capable and beloved by his men, then the spirit that governs the troops may be compared to a vast round stone that rolls from the summit of a mountain down into the valley with furious force.
Sun Tzu: VI. Weakness and Strength
To be first upon the field of battle and there await the enemy is to spare one's strength.
Yet if one is in haste to meet the foe, this is exhausting.
The wise army commander gives heed to this and strives by every means to move the enemy to approach him.
On no account does he allow himself to be deceived by him.
By offering him a seeming advantage, he compels the foe to take up a position which shall likely bring about his defeat.
If the enemy rests in comfortable quarters, then disquiet him.
Appear, therefore, where the enemy is not—attack him at unlooked-for points.
If he has food in abundance, then must thou seek to cut off his supply of provisions.
The point chosen for attack should be kept wholly secret.
If the enemy knows not where he shall be attacked, then must he be prepared in every quarter of the heavens—thus is he everywhere weak.
If the foe sits behind deep moats and strong walls, then strike at such places as compel him to come forth from his hiding.
If a battle is not intended, then take up an unfortified line—the enemy will not dare attack, because thou leavest him in doubt as to thy designs.
Thus is it brought about that thou dost unite, while the foe divides himself.
If the enemy strengthens his front, then must he weaken his rear.
If he reinforces his right wing, then he weakens his left, and the reverse.
To make preparations everywhere is to be weak everywhere—his far-flung preparations weaken him, whilst thou thereby gainest in strength.
If the enemy is very strong, then hinder him from making use of his strength.
Seek to discover what he hath in mind.
Challenge him and learn the measure of his strength.
By making constant feint attacks at divers points, we may awaken in the foe the sense that we are prepared against all assaults and cannot be overcome.
If a battle hath been won by a certain stratagem, then repeat it not, but choose another suited to the circumstances and conditions.
And as the seasons come and go, as the days are short and long, as the moon waxeth and waneth, so also in war there is no constancy—eternal change is its fate.
Sun Tzu: VII. Battle Tactics
The military procedure at first takes its course as follows: the commanding general receives from his sovereign prince the order to make ready for war.
Thereupon he assembles his troops, furnishes himself abundantly with weapons and provisions, and takes particular care that harmony prevails among his men.
Then he takes the field.
Battle tactics are the most difficult part of warfare.
This difficulty consists chiefly in the need to calculate, to judge time, strength, and distance aright.
Nor may the army be overtaken unawares by mischance.

If one can induce the enemy, on his march, to make a detour, hoping thereby to gain some advantage, and then, by setting out after him, arrives at the appointed place before him—such a general is a true master of the art of manoeuvre.
It is scarcely advisable to send the whole army into the field in the belief of thus outwitting such an opponent.
For it may well be that we should not have time enough to accomplish our purpose.
Forced marches are likewise not always to be recommended: for one never knows how many soldiers will arrive at the place sound and fit for action.
As a rule, many a man is left behind enfeebled.
It is also difficult to convey the stores of war, provisions, and the like quickly enough.
Thus a misfortune may very easily occur.
Exact knowledge of the terrain is a great principal matter.
If one is a stranger there, one must by all means take a guide who knows the region well.
Forget not to keep thy movements secret, and await the favourable opportunity.
Swift as the wind should the attack be, but the march quiet, like the silence of the forest.
If thou defendest thyself, then stand firm as the rock in the sea.
The movements, however, should be swift as the lightning.
Drum and bell are therefore employed because the human voice does not suffice to give commands over greater distances.
The flag is used to aid the eye.
When all is ready for the attack, care must be taken that the brave do not stand alone in the foremost ranks—the cowardly must take up battle together with the valiant.
In this wise one may make all soldiers useful.
If the fight takes place during the night, drums and watch-fires are brought into use.
The spirit of the troops is most alert and lively in the morning.
About the noon hour a lassitude and weariness commonly make themselves felt, whereas in the evening one is apt to remain idle.
The wise general, therefore, will not use the time when the vital spirits are most alert—the morning hour—to attack the enemy.
He chooses by preference the noon hours, when the spirits are slack.
Never attack an enemy whose banners flutter gaily in the wind; attack him not either when he encamps upon high terrain or has such at his back.
Never pursue an opponent who only feigns flight.
If thou surroundest him, always leave him an escape route through which he may flee.
Sun Tzu: VIII. Troop Movements
Should the campaign be undertaken in a mountainous region, it is most advisable to pitch camp upon high-lying ground, which must nevertheless lie within the valley.
If rivers must be crossed, then, as soon as you have reached the other bank, do not linger in the river country any longer than is strictly necessary—march on.
If the enemy crosses a river, do not go to meet him, nor attack him while he is still partly upon the water; wait until at least half of the troops have come over.
Leave marshy country as quickly as possible.
If a river or stream has swollen owing to heavy downpours of rain, then wait, and cross it only after the water has subsided again.

Keep far from steep and difficult valleys, likewise from ground that is densely overgrown with thicket and other underbrush, and further from swamps and bogs—endeavour to have them behind you again as quickly as possible.
If you come upon dense forests or upon ground grown high with reeds, search this region thoroughly, since the enemy may perhaps lie there in ambush.
If the adversary is near you, yet conducts himself quietly, then you may surely reckon that he places great confidence in natural means of defence.
But if he encamps upon open ground, this is certain proof that he is right eager for battle.
There are always roads that one should avoid, armed forces that one should not attack, fortresses that one must not besiege, and ground that one must beware of using.
Never encamp in a marshy region.
In mountainous and wooded country, stratagem is perhaps best employed.
Every success depends, of course, upon the skill of the general.
Army commanders must beware of falling into the following dangerous faults: blind haste and reckless foolhardiness; a hot-tempered nature has likewise often wrought great mischief.
If they do not heed these precepts, their defeat may very easily be the consequence.
Sun Tzu: IX. Terrain
In a campaign the nature of the ground is naturally of the very highest importance.
This may be of very diverse kinds.

There is quite open ground; ground that hills and valleys break through, precipices and ravines, narrow passes; but then also ground that stretches away in all directions of the heavens to seemingly endless distances and is as level as a lake.
When one reaches open ground, one should occupy it at once, especially if highland rises in the rear.
Defiles should be occupied without delay; even a force of no great strength can render their capture impossible without great difficulty.
The same holds true of slopes—these should be strongly occupied.
Even able soldiers under the command of incapable officers are ordinarily the cause of general slackness.
On the other hand, soldiers of little worth, though commanded by capable officers, are the cause of defeats.
Weak generals, whose orders are wholly indefinite and whose dispositions may contradict one another, are the reason for great confusion.
Generals who cannot gauge the enemy's strength, who fling small bodies of troops against large ones, who place no picked soldiers in the vanguard, will in all probability be obliged to take flight.
The good general cares for his men with all the means at his command—he is as devoted to them as though they were his own children.
The consequence of this is that they follow him through thick and thin, and in the hour of death they are all at his side.
Yet an excessive care for the soldiers may also have evil consequences: it may cause disobedience; indeed, the men will readily become unfit for service.
They then resemble spoiled children—one can no longer make use of them for anything.
The able general and the soldier who is sent against the enemy—neither draws back.
Their watchword should be: "Know thyself!
Know the enemy!
Then victory is assured thee!"
Sun Tzu: X. War in a Neighbouring Land
Haste and encouragement are the foremost means of keeping up the soldiers' courage in war.
Strike before the enemy is ready, and especially when this can be done from a wholly unexpected quarter.
If the war is waged in a foreign land, it may also be assumed that the soldiers will stand shoulder to shoulder and will therefore seek to avert a defeat with united strength.
Plunder rich plains, so that the troops do not lack good nourishment.
Take proper care also of their health; do not weary them needlessly, but "store up" their health as though each man were a storehouse for it.
If there is no place to which the soldiers might flee, they will not think of running away, but will look death calmly in the eye.
When the soldier sees that death is the only way out, he strains his powers to the utmost.
He knows no fear as soon as he finds himself in a situation from which only desperation can save him.
Forbid the troops to seek to divine the future by signs and omens; no faith should be put in such things.
During the campaign the men must also acquire no riches, not because money and gold are in and of themselves an evil, yet they might easily fall into temptation to make ill use of them.
The true warrior's lot consists in danger, hardship, and exhaustion.
In his nature the soldier should resemble the well-known serpent that dwells in great numbers on the Giant Mountain.
Strike the reptile on the head, and it will still lash you with its tail.
Strike the tail, and it will open its jaws and seek to bite you; strike the middle, and head and tail will unite to do you harm.
Such soldiers also exist!
The first duty of every army leader is to be calm, just, and above all discreet.
He should not reveal his plans even to his officers.
Every change in warfare must remain a deep secret until the moment of its execution.
If the general frequently shifts the position of his camp and takes unexpected roads, no one will be able to guess his plans.
If the troops operate in the interior of the neighbouring land, this is better than if they remain only on the borders.
For there the danger is near that, being not too far from home, they may fall prey to homesickness and run away.
In the interior of the land, by contrast, home does not come strongly to mind, and so there is no longing to be there again.
When an able general attacks a strong neighbouring state, it should also be his first concern to prevent the enemy from concentrating his troops.
He strikes such fear into the foe that other states do not dare to conclude an alliance with the beleaguered party.
Nor does he court the favour of other states; he has full confidence in his own ability and knowledge.
Nevertheless he respects the enemy.
Once war is declared, seek at once to draw advantage from the enemy's weakness.

At first conduct yourself with the modesty and demureness of a young maiden; but if the enemy shows you a small opening, then spring upon him with the liveliness of a rabbit—he will not be able to defend himself.
Sun Tzu: XI. Attack by Fire
To attack the enemy by means of fire, one may employ several methods.
The great and principal matter herein is to await the favourable moment; then, however, one must also have sufficient materials at hand.
Right dry and windy days are best suited to an attack by fire.
The development of such an undertaking must, however, be sharply observed.
If you have succeeded in setting the enemy's camp ablaze, then throw yourself upon him without any delay.
But if you see that the troops remain quiet within the camp, then do not attack, but wait.
The seat of the fire is then not a dangerous one.
A wind that rises by day most often lasts long.
But if it is born by night, it lives but a short while.
Those who lay the fire in the enemy's camp must especially take heed that it may not be easily put out.
A wise sovereign prince, as also a prudent army commander, should ever keep the following points in mind: never fight, except your state be in real danger.
Enter into war only when you believe you may draw advantage from it.
Without prospect of victory, do not stake the lives of your soldiers.
Never arm for war because your heart is for the moment filled with wrath and hatred for this or that reason; these are not of long duration.
If you then come off the worse in war, consider that a land once brought to its knees can only with difficulty raise itself again.
The dead, however, you cannot make alive again.
The wise sovereign prince is therefore very cautious, the prudent general ever on his guard.
If it stands thus with these two, then you need fear nothing for the land; but should the army be forced to battle, it will also surely come forth as victor.

saetze.text: Sun Tzu: XII. The Use of Spies

saetze.kapitel: Suntzu: XII. Die Verwendung von Spionen
saetze.text: With the summoning of a hundred thousand men to arms, very great costs are already incurred.

saetze.kapitel: Suntzu: XII. Die Verwendung von Spionen
saetze.text: It is therefore quite ordinary that the news that the land intends to wage war stirs up strong discontent among the subjects; for they must bear the costs.

saetze.kapitel: Suntzu: XII. Die Verwendung von Spionen
saetze.text: By such a summoning no fewer than a hundred thousand groups are in part greatly disturbed in their accustomed occupations.

saetze.kapitel: Suntzu: XII. Die Verwendung von Spionen
saetze.text: Note: In ancient China the population was divided for military purposes into groups of eight families.

saetze.kapitel: Suntzu: XII. Die Verwendung von Spionen
saetze.text: Each group furnished one man in time of war.

saetze.kapitel: Suntzu: XII. Die Verwendung von Spionen
saetze.text: It also had to see to it that he lacked for nothing; it even cared for his family.

saetze.kapitel: Suntzu: XII. Die Verwendung von Spionen
saetze.text: Thus if a hundred thousand men were levied, a hundred thousand groups were thereby affected.

saetze.kapitel: Suntzu: XII. Die Verwendung von Spionen
saetze.text: But one must also consider that the troops often remain for years in the enemy's land—yet the outcome of the whole war may depend upon a single day.

saetze.kapitel: Suntzu: XII. Die Verwendung von Spionen
Suntzu: XII. Die Verwendung von Spionen
saetze.text: If the sovereign prince is a good man, he will not fleece his subjects' money through a long campaign.

saetze.kapitel: Suntzu: XII. Die Verwendung von Spionen
saetze.text: In order to keep the costs as small as possible, he employs spies.

saetze.kapitel: Suntzu: XII. Die Verwendung von Spionen
saetze.text: Through these he learns the enemy's situation exactly.

saetze.kapitel: Suntzu: XII. Die Verwendung von Spionen
Suntzu: XII. Die Verwendung von Spionen
saetze.text: It is therefore in the very greatest interest of the prince and his general to gain what knowledge they can of the adversary.

saetze.kapitel: Suntzu: XII. Die Verwendung von Spionen
saetze.text: This knowledge, however, is not acquired by calling upon demons and gods, nor does it avail much to consult old experience; only spies are in a position to learn more of these matters.

saetze.kapitel: Suntzu: XII. Die Verwendung von Spionen
saetze.text: There are several kinds of spies.

saetze.kapitel: Suntzu: XII. Die Verwendung von Spionen
saetze.text: If they are used together, then no one can discover the manner in which they "work."

saetze.kapitel: Suntzu: XII. Die Verwendung von Spionen
saetze.text: Most important are the scouts known as "doomed spies," and for the following reasons: if the enemy discovered that he had been deceived by them, they were at once beheaded.

saetze.kapitel: Suntzu: XII. Die Verwendung von Spionen
saetze.text: By name they stood in the service of the enemy, yet in reality they were employed by the adversary, without the enemy's having originally taken him into his service.

saetze.kapitel: Suntzu: XII. Die Verwendung von Spionen
saetze.text: This kind of spy was therefore used first to convey false reports about the foe to the enemy, but then also to spread false tidings among the ranks of the enemy's soldiers.

saetze.kapitel: Suntzu: XII. Die Verwendung von Spionen
saetze.text: Spies should be treated with the greatest courtesy.

saetze.kapitel: Suntzu: XII. Die Verwendung von Spionen
saetze.text: When it comes to the distribution of rewards, the sovereign prince should show generosity toward them.

saetze.kapitel: Suntzu: XII. Die Verwendung von Spionen
Suntzu: XII. Die Verwendung von Spionen
saetze.text: Yet one must watch them most sharply; for it is often difficult to get the truth out of them.

saetze.kapitel: Suntzu: XII. Die Verwendung von Spionen
saetze.text: The power of these spies is quite astonishing.

saetze.kapitel: Suntzu: XII. Die Verwendung von Spionen
saetze.text: They can be used on almost every occasion.

saetze.kapitel: Suntzu: XII. Die Verwendung von Spionen
saetze.text: You must seek to discover the enemy's spies who come into your camp.

saetze.kapitel: Suntzu: XII. Die Verwendung von Spionen
saetze.text: Offer them high sums, which they will certainly accept; make them serviceable to you in any case.

saetze.kapitel: Suntzu: XII. Die Verwendung von Spionen
saetze.text: Only the most skilful men should be employed as spies.

saetze.kapitel: Suntzu: XII. Die Verwendung von Spionen
saetze.text: In every army the spy is a necessary requisite.

saetze.kapitel: Suntzu: XII. Die Verwendung von Spionen
saetze.text: Upon him rest for the most part all movements of the army.

saetze.kapitel: Suntzu: XII. Die Verwendung von Spionen
saetze.text: The prince therefore acts only justly when he distinguishes him, besides high rewards in the form of money, also with outward honours.

saetze.kapitel: Suntzu: XII. Die Verwendung von Spionen
saetze.text: Herewith end the records of Sun Tzu.

saetze.kapitel: Suntzu: XII. Die Verwendung von Spionen
saetze.text: They have not been rendered here word for word.

saetze.kapitel: Suntzu: XII. Die Verwendung von Spionen
saetze.text: The "records" contain a good many things that are no longer of any interest whatsoever.

saetze.kapitel: Suntzu: XII. Die Verwendung von Spionen
saetze.text: It therefore seemed advisable to abridge the original in all places where conditions are spoken of that no longer fit at all even into the present circumstances of China.

saetze.kapitel: Suntzu: XII. Die Verwendung von Spionen
saetze.text: To our knowledge this is also the first attempt to render the records of Sun Tzu in the German tongue.

saetze.kapitel: Wutzu: I. Die Regierung eines Landes
saetze.text: Wu Tzu: I. The Government of a Country

saetze.kapitel: Wutzu: I. Die Regierung eines Landes
saetze.text: In every administration of a state there may be four loud discords, namely: a general discontent; if this be the case, then never engage in a war.

saetze.kapitel: Wutzu: I. Die Regierung eines Landes
saetze.text: Next: a disaffection in the army; then never pitch a camp.

saetze.kapitel: Wutzu: I. Die Regierung eines Landes
saetze.text: Further: discords within the camp itself; then never venture to attack.

saetze.kapitel: Wutzu: I. Die Regierung eines Landes
saetze.text: Lastly: discord in the battle formation; then never suffer matters to come to a decision.

saetze.kapitel: Wutzu: I. Die Regierung eines Landes
saetze.text: Wise princes of the land should therefore first strive to establish harmony among their subjects.

saetze.kapitel: Wutzu: I. Die Regierung eines Landes
saetze.text: Nor is it always advisable for a prince to heed the words of his counsellors—these may easily err.

saetze.kapitel: Wutzu: I. Die Regierung eines Landes
saetze.text: If the subjects know that the ruler is concerned for their welfare and mourns their death most deeply, then even in times of danger the troops will stand ready for battle.

saetze.kapitel: Wutzu: I. Die Regierung eines Landes
saetze.text: In death upon the field of battle they seek their glory.

saetze.kapitel: Wutzu: I. Die Regierung eines Landes
saetze.text: But should they withdraw before the enemy and return home alive, then they would account it a great disgrace and shame.

saetze.kapitel: Wutzu: I. Die Regierung eines Landes
saetze.text: It must ever be the aim of the government of a country to protect undertakings of every kind and to preserve the state from every misfortune.

saetze.kapitel: Wutzu: I. Die Regierung eines Landes
saetze.text: Practise therefore righteousness; let prudence and wisdom mark all thy actions; kindness and benevolence will dispose the people favourably.

saetze.kapitel: Wutzu: I. Die Regierung eines Landes
saetze.text: Upon a government of a land, as upon the commanding general, these should ever be impressed: morality, sense of duty, righteousness, self-control, lawfulness, nobility of mind, and sincerity.

saetze.kapitel: Wutzu: I. Die Regierung eines Landes
saetze.text: But the sense of shame must above all be fostered.

saetze.kapitel: Wutzu: I. Die Regierung eines Landes
saetze.text: If this be proper to the troops, then will they also, if strong enough, attack with great resolution, and, if weaker, defend themselves to the uttermost.

saetze.kapitel: Wutzu: I. Die Regierung eines Landes
saetze.text: If we follow the course of history, we shall find that nations which have won several great victories have through this seeming advantage very often grown quite frail—a decline is to be recorded.

saetze.kapitel: Wutzu: I. Die Regierung eines Landes
saetze.text: Other states, even if they were less victorious, grew impoverished.

saetze.kapitel: Wutzu: I. Die Regierung eines Landes
saetze.text: A few victories were usually enough to found a kingdom.

saetze.kapitel: Wutzu: I. Die Regierung eines Landes
saetze.text: Small is the number of those on earth who, by winning many victories, attained to great power.

saetze.kapitel: Wutzu: I. Die Regierung eines Landes
saetze.text: But very many have lost everything through too great success in war.

saetze.kapitel: Wutzu: I. Die Regierung eines Landes
saetze.text: The causes that lead to war may for the most part be traced to the following: ambition of the prince of the land; the craving to draw advantage; an excess of passing hatred; inward confusion; national misfortune, such as droughts, famine, and the like.

saetze.kapitel: Wutzu: I. Die Regierung eines Landes
Wutzu: I. Die Regierung eines Landes
saetze.text: By nature there are just wars, then such as where the aggressor relies upon his strength; but revenge also may be the motive; lastly: unrighteous campaigns.

saetze.kapitel: Wutzu: I. Die Regierung eines Landes
Wutzu: I. Die Regierung eines Landes
saetze.text: Draw to thee the wise of thy land and empower them to take part in the government of the state.

saetze.kapitel: Wutzu: I. Die Regierung eines Landes
saetze.text: But give the foolish wholly subordinate posts.

saetze.kapitel: Wutzu: I. Die Regierung eines Landes
saetze.text: If thou dost this, then mayest thou also rely upon thine army.

saetze.kapitel: Wutzu: I. Die Regierung eines Landes
Wutzu: I. Die Regierung eines Landes
saetze.text: If the subjects have no cares, but full confidence, if they are devoted to their superiors, then the land also has a strong, albeit invisible, wall of defence.

saetze.kapitel: Wutzu: I. Die Regierung eines Landes
saetze.text: Into all hearts a feeling of security enters; fears remain far off.

saetze.kapitel: Wutzu: I. Die Regierung eines Landes
saetze.text: Only there, where the citizens look with full trust upon their prince and know how to esteem his abilities—only there can that happiness be at home in a state which forms the sole source of contentment among the subjects.
Wu Tzu: II. Estimating the Enemy
In the life of nations it often comes to pass that a country is threatened by several of its neighbouring states at once.
Then, indeed, it is needful to be right watchful.

But if the sovereign prince has an able army commander, and his counsellors are serviceable men, they will for the most part find that none of these states is strong enough to become dangerous—all have their weaknesses.
Thus the armed forces of one state may be considerable, yet they lack tenacity and cohesion.
The troops of another country roam about scattered and would fight on their own in case of war.
The constitution of another state's army is good, yet it could not hold out for long.
The troops of still other lands might well be able to defend themselves ably, yet they lack the courage, resolution, and daring to advance.
The government of such neighbouring lands itself likewise leaves much to be desired in many respects.

This state may be rich, but obstinacy and hard-heartedness prevail; the prince and his officials are proud and dissolute, and they take no care for the common people; rewards and honours are dispensed with partiality.
In another state we find again that opinions in the camp are much divided, that discord prevails, and it lacks steadfastness.
Another state is very large.
But for that very reason the government is weak; it can but poorly oversee its officials.
The troops are indeed in good condition, yet they lack endurance.
To subjugate such a land is therefore not difficult.

Still other lands are wholly peaceable, and the government is also just; should it come to war, however, the citizens would raise objection against it: past experience has taught them that a war, even the most successful, is at bottom a great national misfortune.
The troops are well trained, but generals and officers are despised, either because they are incapable or dissolute.
Since the soldiers' pay is but small, they also lack the spirit of self-sacrifice.
Of such troops one must not expect much in case of war; the enemy for the most part has easy work with them.
Attack the enemy that has set out early in the harshness of winter and, though wholly benumbed, yet offers his brow to the tempest.

But an enemy also that begins his march in the glowing morning heat of summer, that perhaps suffers great thirst and hunger and nevertheless strives to reach a certain place—him you may attack as well.
If you have before you an enemy whose camp has not changed its place for a long time and who can no longer collect provisions from the country people, then he too is powerless.
Defeat is certain for this reason alone, because the men have lost confidence in their officers.

If the enemy has taken an exposed position, or if he is passing through difficult ground, then attack him undauntedly, especially if the camp is not yet fully pitched or the battle formation not yet ordered.
Under these and like conditions the enemy's defeat is as certain as the ebb and flow of the tide, as the rising and setting of the stars, as the sky must bring us sunshine and gloomy days.

Very great territories whose population is rich and numerous; regions in which the officials meet the citizens with benevolence; where rewards are dispensed in a just manner and the guilty are justly punished; lands that are themselves strong and that in time of need can always draw allies to them—such regions avoid, if you are operating in enemy country.

The enemy's defeat is determined under the following conditions: if he approaches you carelessly, if his banners are in disorder, if his order of march is also faulty, then a panic will doubtless seize him when you attack him.
The chief matter, however, remains always that you know the true condition of the enemy exactly—then strike at once at his weak points.
If an enemy has made a long forced march and his ranks are not yet ordered, he is easily wounded.
If he does not make proper use of the ground on which he camps, if he crosses a narrow stretch of ground, then he is powerless and must surrender.

saetze.kapitel: Wutzu: III. Die Ueberwachung der Armee
saetze.text: Wu Tzu: III. The Oversight of the Army

saetze.kapitel: Wutzu: III. Die Ueberwachung der Armee
saetze.text: In a campaign it is of the highest importance that all things move with ease and suppleness.

saetze.kapitel: Wutzu: III. Die Ueberwachung der Armee
saetze.text: To this end the roads must be good, for the wagons must not be hindered by bad highways.

saetze.kapitel: Wutzu: III. Die Ueberwachung der Armee
saetze.text: If this be so, then much is already gained.

saetze.kapitel: Wutzu: III. Die Ueberwachung der Armee
saetze.text: Impartiality must prevail; rewards should be allotted to those who have deserved them, for thus the troops are spurred on the more.

saetze.kapitel: Wutzu: III. Die Ueberwachung der Armee
saetze.text: Since discipline in the host is the anchor of safety, the guilty must be punished without mercy.

saetze.kapitel: Wutzu: III. Die Ueberwachung der Armee
saetze.text: But that an army may remain victorious, it is altogether necessary that the government of the land be a good one.

saetze.kapitel: Wutzu: III. Die Ueberwachung der Armee
saetze.text: The laws must be just.

saetze.kapitel: Wutzu: III. Die Ueberwachung der Armee
saetze.text: Above all, however, order must prevail everywhere.

saetze.kapitel: Wutzu: III. Die Ueberwachung der Armee
saetze.text: If this be so, unity cannot be destroyed, even when grave dangers threaten.

saetze.kapitel: Wutzu: III. Die Ueberwachung der Armee
saetze.text: On the march the resting places must be observed as far as possible; men and beasts must not be exhausted.

saetze.kapitel: Wutzu: III. Die Ueberwachung der Armee
saetze.text: All these things a good general must oversee with the utmost conscientiousness.

saetze.kapitel: Wutzu: III. Die Ueberwachung der Armee
saetze.text: Delay, however, is his greatest enemy.

saetze.kapitel: Wutzu: III. Die Ueberwachung der Armee
Wutzu: III. Die Ueberwachung der Armee
saetze.text: Irresolution brings to birth the misfortune by which an army is beset.

saetze.kapitel: Wutzu: III. Die Ueberwachung der Armee
saetze.text: Soldiers in many cases meet their death because they:

saetze.kapitel: Wutzu: III. Die Ueberwachung der Armee
Wutzu: III. Die Ueberwachung der Armee
saetze.text: lack all understanding of how they are to conduct themselves.

saetze.kapitel: Wutzu: III. Die Ueberwachung der Armee
saetze.text: Constant practice is therefore a chief necessity.

saetze.kapitel: Wutzu: III. Die Ueberwachung der Armee
saetze.text: Attack the enemy, if in any way possible, at short distance.

saetze.kapitel: Wutzu: III. Die Ueberwachung der Armee
saetze.text: Men who come from one and the same district of their homeland should be placed in one and the same detachment; thus they hold together the more firmly.

saetze.kapitel: Wutzu: III. Die Ueberwachung der Armee
saetze.text: If in any way possible, avoid on the march "natural ovens" (that is to say, entrances to great valleys), and next "dragons' heads" (spurs of mountain ranges).

saetze.kapitel: Wutzu: III. Die Ueberwachung der Armee
saetze.text: Thou must also, when thou marchest into battle, study the direction of the wind.

saetze.kapitel: Wutzu: III. Die Ueberwachung der Armee
saetze.text: If it blows against the enemy, then follow the wind with thy troops.

saetze.kapitel: Wutzu: III. Die Ueberwachung der Armee
saetze.text: But if a contrary wind prevails, it is advisable to strengthen thy positions yet further.

saetze.kapitel: Wutzu: III. Die Ueberwachung der Armee
saetze.text: Wait until the wind has abated or shifted.
Wu Tzu: IV. Qualities of a General
The leader of an army should not only be a master of the art of war, but also a good scholar of literature and the sciences.
He who is upright and undaunted, yet at the same time concerned for the welfare of his men, to him may an army be entrusted.
Courage and boldness alone do not suffice in a general.
All too great a confidence in oneself often breeds carelessness and inattention.
Should the general have acted rashly, he must not boast of it, even if the outcome was a fortunate one, for one can never be certain of the result.
Resoluteness before the enemy buries all thoughts of sparing this life.
Even after a victory one must exercise great caution.
When the general draws into battle, it is likewise his sacred duty not to return until he has smitten the foe.
In death upon the field of battle he should seek his highest glory.
Never should he return to his homeland, save as a victor who has saved his country.
The worth of an army, though it may be hundreds of thousands strong, depends upon a single man, the supreme commander.
This is the consequence of the influence of understanding and discernment.
When one takes the field, the great secret lies in knowing what the abilities of the enemy commander are.
If he is a man of narrow mind and trusts carelessly in the future, he may without difficulty be lured into a snare by cunning.
If he is covetous and sets no store by his good name, he may easily be bribed.
If the higher officers are rich and proud, while those beneath them are poor, grasping, and vengeful, then spies should stir these up against their superiors.
Under such conditions it is not hard to render the enemy unfit for battle and thus bring the campaign to a fortunate conclusion.

saetze.kapitel: Wutzu: V. Das Anpassen an die Gelegenheit
saetze.text: Wu Tzu: V. Adapting to the Occasion

saetze.kapitel: Wutzu: V. Das Anpassen an die Gelegenheit
saetze.text: In war it often happens that the armies facing one another as enemies are unequal in number; then the chief rule is always to avoid the enemy on large and open ground.

saetze.kapitel: Wutzu: V. Das Anpassen an die Gelegenheit
saetze.text: If the terrain is confined, then you may well venture to meet him.

saetze.kapitel: Wutzu: V. Das Anpassen an die Gelegenheit
saetze.text: Even small bodies of troops can easily defend passes, gorges, and hollows.

saetze.kapitel: Wutzu: V. Das Anpassen an die Gelegenheit
saetze.text: But if you have considerable hosts at your disposal, then seek out plains; in the contrary case, however, seek narrow ground.

saetze.kapitel: Wutzu: V. Das Anpassen an die Gelegenheit
saetze.text: If a small force appears unexpectedly in such ground, then even a strong enemy who finds himself facing this opponent will be struck with great fear as soon as he hears drums and gongs sounded loudly.

saetze.kapitel: Wutzu: V. Das Anpassen an die Gelegenheit
saetze.text: Perhaps he will even withdraw quickly.

saetze.kapitel: Wutzu: V. Das Anpassen an die Gelegenheit
Wutzu: V. Das Anpassen an die Gelegenheit
saetze.text: Now it may also happen that you unexpectedly encounter the enemy in a valley of small extent.

saetze.kapitel: Wutzu: V. Das Anpassen an die Gelegenheit
saetze.text: The terrain is altogether mountainous; the enemy's force is large, while you yourself are not overly strong.

saetze.kapitel: Wutzu: V. Das Anpassen an die Gelegenheit
saetze.text: In this case, sound the drum first and attack; do not hesitate!

saetze.kapitel: Wutzu: V. Das Anpassen an die Gelegenheit
saetze.text: Send your core troops against him.

saetze.kapitel: Wutzu: V. Das Anpassen an die Gelegenheit
saetze.text: Since large masses of troops are useless in such ground, it is also to be supposed that the enemy will assume a waiting posture, for he does not know your strength.

saetze.kapitel: Wutzu: V. Das Anpassen an die Gelegenheit
saetze.text: You yourself, however, must pretend as though you were preparing everything for an attack; this is naturally only a feint maneuver, for in reality your troops withdraw as unnoticed as possible through the pass into the open ground lying behind it, and there you pitch camp.

saetze.kapitel: Wutzu: V. Das Anpassen an die Gelegenheit
saetze.text: The enemy, however, will be so deceived—he himself likely fears an attack—that he pays no further attention to your withdrawal.

saetze.kapitel: Wutzu: V. Das Anpassen an die Gelegenheit
saetze.text: By such a stratagem you save your people from death and ruin, and you are thereby afforded the opportunity, perhaps at the very next occasion, to see your troops emerge honourably from battle and combat.
Wu Tzu: Afterword
Here end the "Sayings" of Wu Tzu.
As a literary creation they can in no wise compare with the "Records" of Sun Tzu, quite apart from the fact that they are far from being as extensive.
As a successful army commander, Wu Tzu's fame was known far beyond the borders of that state in which he passed the greater part of his life.
This was the state of Wei.
As it is said, he won for the ruling prince above sixty victories in wars waged against neighbouring states.
Hereby the boundaries of the state of Wei were most considerably enlarged.
As was already remarked at the outset, this general was in his ordinary life by no means a man of high moral standing.
To cite but a few examples:
Thus he slew two of his wives for the simple reason that they were born in a state with which the prince in whose service he stood was waging war.
Wu Tzu feared, namely, that his army might suspect him of secretly taking the part of the princes of those lands.
But what, at least in the eyes of the Chinese, placed Wu Tzu so low morally was the fact that he was not present at the deathbed and bier of his mother, although nothing hindered him from being so.
Such a deed the Chinese hold to be a deadly sin, which can by nothing be expiated.
Ancient Chinese War Songs
Among the oldest war songs handed down to us are those of the Chinese people.
They have been preserved for us in the "Schiking," the so-called "Book of Songs."
Their average age may be estimated at nearly 3000 years.
Similar collections, of roughly the same age and standing, we have only in the Psalms of the Hebrews and the Rigveda of the Indians.

Note: The songs contained in the "Schiking," about 300 in number, were collected and completed toward the end of the 5th century B.C. by the great Chinese sage Confucius, whom the missionaries Latinized as Confucius.
If the Chinese of the present day are anything but warlike in disposition, in ancient times it was otherwise.
Almost constantly it came to armed conflicts, if not with the neighboring states, then with the wild tribes and hordes that sought to harass the realm from the north and south.
It is only natural, then, that these campaigns gave occasion for songs, which were sung especially at court on festive occasions.
When in those ancient times the military force was drawn up, the leaders of all ranks as well as the chariot fighters—there was no riding at all—were taken from the educated class.
For a distinction such as exists in China at present—between civil and military officials—did not take place.
The numerous foot soldiers were raised by the levy of the able-bodied settled population.

Since these were then suddenly torn from their ordered lives, from their livelihoods and family circumstances, it explains why we so often encounter in the "War Songs" laments over the hardships and privations of the campaigns, over the disrupted domestic conditions, over the vain longing for home.
The men therefore went unwillingly to war and openly admitted it.
The battles themselves and brilliant victories, however, also called forth again a warlike enthusiasm, as several of the following songs attest.
The firm confidence in the continuation of life after death, in the connection with those left behind that still endured even then, could only make fearless and death-defying fighters.
The military system was in any case very well ordered for cases of war.
Weapons of all kinds, war chariots, battle standards and other war equipment had to be kept in store and in good condition in the arsenals.
Four times a year, namely in the middle of each season, weapons exercises and larger field exercises took place.
In connection with the "Book of War" it may be of interest to make a small selection from the many songs relating to war that the "Schiking" contains.
The best translation we have is the one published by Victor von Strauß.
It is as faithful as possible in sense and word; it also shows a reproduction of the foreign form approximated as closely as possible.
Note: "Schiking, the Canonical Book of Songs of the Chinese."
Translated and explained by Victor von Strauß, Heidelberg.
Carl Winter's University Bookshop.

The following selection, however, shows deviations in some places from the above-named translation—several reasons seemed to us to speak for this—yet the content and the formal garb have been only slightly affected thereby.
Hopefully they correspond to their special purpose, and if this is achieved, then these poems will have fully served their purpose in this place as well.
B. N. The Warrior's Lot

What herb is here not scorched yellow?

And on what day is there no running?

And what man is not sent forth

To service and toil in every land?
Note: Namely: as a result of the devastation caused by war.

What herb is here that is not blackened?

And what man whom something does not pain?

Woe unto us dispatched people,

Are we but cast out from the folk?

Neither tame nor wild beast,

We traverse desolate steppes here.

Woe unto us dispatched people,

From early till late we do not rest!
Song of Victory

Three thousand were his chariots,

His host proven in resistance.

The troops were led by Fangshu's hand;

And there upon fresh-ploughed fields

He drove with his team of white horses,

The red of the chariot shows the rank.

With screen-wall, shining fish-skin quiver

And breast-harness and bridle-trappings.
Note: The four steeds, with which one mostly drove, were harnessed side by side—the two inner ones to the shaft, while the two outer ones, with somewhat shorter traces, ran more freely.
The reins of these

Three thousand were his chariots,

War banners fluttered among them,

Yoke-ornament and side-band showed finely

There on the new river-banks.

Brightly clinked eight bridle-bells,

Young Shu wore the high robe of office,

The chariot's passage gave splendor and sheen,

Thus he found nowhere resistance.T)
Note: In the original it says: "The dragon banners and the serpent—as well as tortoise banners fluttered."
Note: The band on the wheel-hubs was an ornament of red leather.
went through sliding rings that were fastened to the breast-harness of the shaft-horses.
Red was the color of the Chou dynasty, thus shows the rank: a royal team.
T) Fangshu, the leader against the barbarian tribes in the south of the realm, marched out in the year 825

Three thousand were his chariots;

With cymbal-strikers, drum-sounds

He arrayed the hosts, he guided multitudes

On freshly broken plough-lands.

However high he stood in years,

So bold yet were his designs.

The drumbeat sounded dull and fearful,

Home drew the host with merry sound.
Note: Dull and deep was the drumbeat in battle; merry and bright-sounding at the victorious homecoming.

Three thousand were his war chariots;

Long lasted the decisive battle,

Yet the enemy gave way before the superior force

On blood-soaked field-layers.

He chastised the wild hordes,

Insolent was the evildoers' hostile bearing.

Like cloud-crash and thunder-sound

Let therefore ring the song of victory!
Note: The evildoers are the chieftains of the vanquished who are to be subjected to torture.
B.C. against these.
The song is accordingly over 2700 years old.
Song of Praise of the Warriors after the Campaign

Our axes are broken,

Our hatchets are shattered;

The King's compassion for us people

Shows itself above all now.

Our axes are broken,

Our chisels are shattered;

The King's compassion for us people

Shows itself now in full splendor.
Note: The "chisel" was a very old and simple weapon.
The song falls in the years 1122 – 1114 B.C.

Our axes are broken,

Our clubs are smashed;

The King's compassion for us people

Is the most glorious thing in the world!
Song of the Campaign

O would we were home, O would we were home!

Yet well a year has then passed by,

And rest and repose are excluded,

The while the Huns have poured forth;

When shall we go home, when shall we go home?

O would we were home, O would we were home!
Note: The Huns, at that time known under the name "Hiungnu," troubled the north of the realm at the end of the 10th century B.C.
The origin of this song also falls in this time.

Sorrowful hearts burn here,

Now we hunger and now we thirst,

The homesickness, it consumes us well-nigh;

When shall we go home, when shall we go home?

O would we were home, O would we were home!

Yet the King's service wants no sluggards,

We may not indulge in rest,

Onward it goes on pathless ways.

When shall we go home, when shall we go home?
Note: Until the end of this stanza the supreme commander is not yet with the warriors—hence the

But what comes driving on the road there?

That is the host-prince's chariot!

Now it behooves us to fight gloriously,

And behold! The victory we carry off!

And proud upon us the King looked!

And thrice victorious was the battle!

Who was there who was not heated for the fight?

Upon us the host-prince leans,

It is the warrior who protects the land!

We are the realm's strong watch!

Now that we go homeward again,

Thirst and hunger are not to be avoided,

The march is long and not to be envied,

And no one knows of our sufferings.

What of it? We shall see home again!
Note: dejected mood, which at his appearance (in the fourth stanza) transforms into certainty of victory.
The Warrior's Reception in His Own Home
Note: It is assumed that the women greeted the returning warriors with this song, which depicts the longing for their return.

The King's service brooks no neglect!

In the tenth moon are moon and sun,

And our days go on and on.
Note: The women fear the tenth moon would still find the men in the field.

The women's hearts are wound about with grief,

O were the time of war run out!

The King's service brooks no neglect!

Though herb and tree deck themselves in green—

The heart breaks with woe and sorrow,

The women's hearts are full of grieving.

O that the warriors would come again!

The King's service brooks no neglect!

Still the warriors have remained far off,

And our parents suffer pain.

Is it because the stallions are worn down?

The sandalwood chariots are ground to pieces?
Note: During a campaign in a foreign land the soldier was not permitted to maintain any connection with the families left behind, even only to inquire after their well-being.

The King's service brooks no neglect!

Not yet have the warriors returned home,

And greater grow our sorrows.

And yet—behold! The victors draw near!

Upon our hearts rest the warriors!
Victorious Campaign

To war it went with hot desire,

War chariots all in readiness,

Many a team of stallions stamped and sprang,

Armor was packed with garments too,

The enemies were wildly aflame,

And we therefore in haste's own fire.

Into the field the King sends the host,

To free his lands.

The black horses were all of equal strength,

With proudly lifted heads they went.
Note: This song likewise falls in the first reign of Sin An; his commander was Kifu,
Note: Four horses of equal excellence were always harnessed together.
Note: The women think the warriors are surely approaching, and only have not yet arrived because the horses and chariots (of sandalwood) have suffered so much from the campaign.

Though our march was long and far—

Struck down is the enemy of the North.

The warriors are full of gladness,

Kifu had united them.

Whether war, whether peace in the land:

A model for every man

Is Kifu's skilled warrior-hand—

Therefore a red team also honors him.†)
Brotherhood in Arms

Who says thou hast no garment?

My clothes, they are thine too!

The King sets the host in readiness,

I provide for pikes and lances fine,

Thou shalt be my brother-in-arms!

Who says thou hast no garment?

My clothes, we share them!

The King sets the host in readiness,

I provide for pikes and spears here,

And break forth united with thee!

Who says thou hast no garment?

With thee I share my soldier's garb.

The King sets the host in readiness,

Make weapons and arms already ready,

And march out with thee to the strife!
†) A war chariot whose horses had red harness, whose wheels were also painted red, counted as a very high royal distinction.
The War Hero's Wife

I think of my noble lord!

His war chariot, what splendor!

On the shaft-beam hanging ornaments,

On the side-board gold-ringed traces,

The tiger-skin, the little bells' ringing.

It grips me into the deepest heart,

That now a house of boards alone is his.

I think of my noble lord!

Four stallions go in proud magnificence,

Six reins are brought to hand.

Sawest thou ever dappled greys more spirited?

At the front of the chariot the dragon-images.

O, how I think of him so much;

When comes the time of return?
I think of my high lord!

Note: Verses two to five of each stanza of this song depict the warlike equipment of the husband at his departure, as he ever hovers before the singer's eyes; in the last ones she then passes in a rapid leap to her present feelings.

The steeds in armor, equal in strength,

The golden shaft of the trident-spear,

The proud tiger-case at the bow,

That bore his two bows.

His fame of virtue shall ever endure.

At rising and at lying down to sleep

I think of my noble lord!
Note: The white ribbons that flutter down from the banners are meant.
